mcqs.question: What determines whether an interaction should be request-response or event-driven?
options: Whether the caller's own flow blocks on the result, and whether multiple independent parties need to react
Whether the action itself is inherently fast or slow to execute
Whether the two services are owned by the same team
Whether the interaction happens more or less than once per second
mcqs.explanation: The deciding factor is whether the caller needs the answer to proceed and how many independent reactors exist — not the action's raw speed, team ownership, or call frequency, none of which determine the right interaction shape on their own.

mcqs.question: Checkout publishes an `order_placed` event that fraud-scoring subscribes to instead of being called synchronously. What capability does checkout give up as a result?
options: The ability to know synchronously whether the fraud check passed
The ability to add more subscribers to the order_placed event later
The ability to process orders at all if fraud-scoring is down
The ability to log that an order was placed
mcqs.explanation: Decoupling checkout from fraud-scoring means checkout can no longer get a synchronous answer about the fraud check's outcome — that's the direct cost of the pattern. It doesn't limit adding future subscribers (the opposite is true), doesn't block checkout if fraud-scoring is down (that's the resilience benefit), and logging is unrelated.

mcqs.question: The business wants a single "order status" view spanning five event-driven services, without giving up the decoupling on the write path. What's the right approach?
options: Revert every write to synchronous calls so status can be queried live
Build a materialized view/read model that subscribes to all five services' events and aggregates state
Pick one of the five services to own the canonical status and have the others call it synchronously
Have the client poll all five services directly and merge the results itself
mcqs.explanation: A materialized view keeps the write path fully event-driven while giving the read path one fast, pre-aggregated place to answer status queries. Reverting to synchronous writes throws away the decoupling that was the point, and pushing the aggregation to a single service or the client either reintroduces coupling or duplicates fan-out logic client-side.

mcqs.question: A team declares "our architecture is event-driven" and applies that pattern to every interaction, including ones where a caller needs an immediate answer to proceed. What's wrong with that?
options: Nothing — a consistent architectural style is always preferable to mixing patterns
It loses the ability to reason about a request's end-to-end outcome exactly where the caller genuinely needed a synchronous result
Event-driven systems cannot technically support any interaction that needs a fast response
It would require rewriting every service in a different programming language
mcqs.explanation: Applying event-driven as a blanket rule breaks the cases where the caller's own flow truly depends on the result — those need request-response regardless of the rest of the architecture's style. A single system can legitimately mix both patterns; event-driven doesn't technically forbid fast responses, and language choice is unrelated to this decision.
